summary: Defines a YANG module called ietf-keystore for centrally configuring symmetric and asymmetric keys on a device. The secret values can be encrypted or hidden, and asymmetric keys can be tied to certificates. Like its companion truststore module, it can notify when certificates are close to expiring.

eli5.summary: Think of a locked cupboard where a device keeps its secret keys, each with a label. Other settings can ask for a key by name, and the cupboard tells you when a key's ID card is running out.

subtitle: A YANG module for keeping a device's symmetric and asymmetric keys, and their certificates, in one place.

tldr.problem: Network devices need cryptographic keys for SSH, TLS and similar uses, and there was no common YANG way to configure them centrally, protect their secret values, or tie keys to certificates.
tldr.mechanism: The ietf-keystore YANG module defines a keystore holding symmetric and asymmetric keys. Each secret can be stored in cleartext, hidden (for hardware-protected keys) or encrypted by another key, and asymmetric keys can carry certificates. Groupings let other modules take a key inline or by reference.
tldr.outcome: Operators get one model for keys and certificates, with a notification when a certificate is about to expire and an action to generate a certificate signing request.

today: RFC 9642 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2024 and has not been obsoleted. It builds on the crypto-types module in RFC 9640 and sits beside the truststore module in RFC 9641.

sections.title: What the Keystore Is For
sections.content:
RFC 9642 presents a YANG 1.1 module called ietf-keystore for centralized configuration of symmetric and asymmetric keys. The secret value of either type may be encrypted or hidden, and asymmetric keys may be associated with certificates. In this document a keystore is a mechanism that intends to safeguard secrets.

The module also defines many groupings for other modules to import, for instance groupings that let a key be configured inline or as a reference to a key in the central keystore.

It is part of a collection of RFCs that together support configuring clients and servers of NETCONF and RESTCONF. It depends on the crypto-types module from RFC 9640, and the truststore module of RFC 9641 is a sibling that uses the same base.

The document aims to reflect existing practice. Implementations may use operating-system keystores or cryptographic hardware such as a trusted platform module (TPM).
sections.eli5: It gives devices one tidy, standard place to keep their secret keys and ID cards instead of every feature keeping its own.

sections.title: The Data Model
sections.content:
The top-level keystore container has two parts. asymmetric-keys is a list of keys, each with a name, public key, private key and a list of certificates. symmetric-keys is a list of named symmetric keys. Four features control what a server implements: central-keystore-supported, inline-definitions-supported, asymmetric-keys and symmetric-keys.

The private part of an asymmetric key, and the value of a symmetric key, is a choice of three forms: cleartext, hidden (an empty leaf, for keys the hardware never reveals) or encrypted. An encrypted value names the key that encrypted it (encrypted-by), the format and the encrypted bytes.

Each certificate has a name and its data. The module defines a certificate-expiration notification carrying an expiration-date, sent when a certificate is about to expire, and a generate-csr action that returns a PKCS#10 request, available under the csr-generation feature.
sections.eli5: Each key in the cupboard has a name tag. Its secret part is either written out, locked away where nobody can read it, or sealed in an envelope that another key can open.

sections.title: Groupings for Other Modules
sections.content:
The module offers groupings other YANG modules can reuse. Four of them, such as inline-or-keystore-asymmetric-key-grouping, present a choice: define the key inline (using a crypto-types grouping from RFC 9640) or point to a key in the central keystore with a leafref typedef. Another, central-asymmetric-key-certificate-ref-grouping, refers to a certificate in two parts: the key's name and the certificate's name.

The keystore-grouping grouping defines a keystore instance, separate from the top-level node, so a consuming module may instantiate a keystore elsewhere. The RFC calls the top-level instance the central keystore. Additional cases may be augmented in to reference keys in alternate locations.
sections.eli5: Other settings can either carry their own key or just say 'use the key named so-and-so from the cupboard'.

sections.title: Built-In Keys
sections.content:
A server may have keys built in. They may be set during manufacturing, or generated the first time the server boots or a service such as SSH is enabled. Built-in keys are hidden keys set by a vendor-specific process, and how operators might change them is outside the scope of the RFC.

Because the server provides them rather than an operator configuring them, they appear in <operational> with the origin annotation or:system. Typically such a key is paired with an identity certificate, for example an Initial Device Identifier (IDevID) certificate.

The RFC shows how a built-in key can be propagated into <running> so that an operator can add a deployment-specific LDevID certificate next to the manufacturer's IDevID certificate.
sections.eli5: Some devices come with a special key already locked inside from the factory. You can add your own ID card for it, but you cannot take the key out.

sections.title: Encrypting Keys in Configuration
sections.content:
This section is not normative. It explains how a configuration containing encrypted secrets can be backed up from one server and restored on another when each server has unique primary keys.

The scheme rests on a key encryption key (KEK), a key that encrypts other keys. A KEK may be symmetric or asymmetric. Each new key SHOULD be encrypted by a KEK, and servers SHOULD offer an API that generates a key and encrypts it in one step so administrators never see the cleartext.

To move a configuration, the second server needs the same KEK. Rather than depending on crypto officers each time, a special KEK called the primary key (PK) can be used. A PK is commonly a globally unique built-in asymmetric key with a hidden private part and a public half in an identity certificate. A crypto officer can encrypt one shared KEK offline for many servers using their public keys. To migrate, an administrator swaps in the shared KEK encrypted for the second server, and the rest of the configuration loads unchanged.
sections.eli5: Keys are put in sealed envelopes. A trusted person makes one copy of the master envelope key for each device, so you can move all the other envelopes between devices without opening them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Server implementations are RECOMMENDED to encrypt keystore contents when persisted to non-volatile memory and to zeroize decrypted contents in volatile memory when not in use. Storing cleartext values is NOT RECOMMENDED; if it is done, persistence-layer encryption SHOULD be used. If contents are not encrypted when persisted, implementations MUST ensure the storage is inaccessible.

The module does not constrain what operations a private key may be used for, nor the use of public keys except through a configured certificate, where the certificate limits the usage.

Access to the module is expected over secure management protocols such as NETCONF and RESTCONF, with access control from the Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM). The cleartext-symmetric-key and cleartext-private-key nodes should never be returned to a client in normal use, so they are marked default-deny-all in RFC 9640. All writable nodes in this module are marked default-deny-write. Built-in keys SHOULD be hidden or encrypted.
sections.eli5: Keep the cupboard locked, wipe any key you pulled out when you are done, and only let trusted people look inside or change things.

viz.caption: THE THREE FORMS OF A SECRET KEY VALUE

items.title: Cleartext
items.text: The raw key value is stored as is. Not recommended; sensitive to reads.

items.title: Hidden
items.text: An empty leaf. The secret is kept by hardware and never revealed, as with built-in keys.

items.title: Encrypted
items.text: The value is encrypted by a symmetric or asymmetric key in the keystore, such as a KEK.
